# California Didn't Lose Larry Page. It Drove Him Out Before the Law Even Passed.

That distinction matters more than most people realize.

Paul Graham confirmed what the tech world had been whispering: Larry Page has permanently left California. Not a Florida domicile trick. Not a paper relocation. Gone. And the wealth tax that triggered it hasn't even been enacted yet.

Let that land. The chilling effect of a *proposed* policy already cost California the physical presence and future tax contributions of one of the wealthiest individuals on the planet. The law didn't need to pass. The credibility of the threat was enough.

This is the part that should keep every founder and operator up at night.

---

**Policy risk is now priced into location decisions the same way it's priced into cap tables.**

Founders don't wait for a bad term sheet to close before walking away from a deal. They read the signal and move. That's exactly what's happening with California geography right now. The founders and capital allocators paying closest attention are making relocation decisions based on the *trajectory* of policy, not just the current state of it. When your planning horizon is a decade, the direction of travel matters more than today's rate.

---

**The tax revenue math is backwards — and California keeps getting it wrong.**

The stated goal of a wealth tax is to capture more revenue from concentrated capital. The actual outcome, playing out in real time, is that the wealthiest and most mobile individuals simply leave — taking their future income, investment activity, philanthropy, and economic footprint with them. You don't collect more revenue from someone who no longer lives there. You collect zero. The state is trading a fraction of something enormous for the entirety of nothing.

---

**This accelerates a flywheel that's already spinning.**

When a figure of Larry Page's magnitude exits, it doesn't just remove one taxpayer. It sends a permission structure to the next tier of founders and executives who were watching to see how serious the risk was. His departure is a data point that validates the concern and lowers the social friction of leaving. Miami, Austin, Dubai, and a handful of other jurisdictions are not winning on merit alone — they're winning because California keeps making the exit decision easier.

---

**What this means if you're building right now:**

Your incorporation state, your team's physical location, and your personal domicile are no longer just administrative decisions. They are strategic ones. If you're recruiting senior talent to the Bay Area, you need to have an honest conversation about the policy environment you're asking them to build their financial future inside. If you're choosing where to headquarter a new venture, California's brand prestige no longer automatically outweighs its policy risk.

The infrastructure of the Bay Area — the density of talent, capital, and institutional knowledge — remains real. But infrastructure depreciates when the operators who built it keep leaving and the policy environment discourages their replacements from staying.

Larry Page leaving before the law passed isn't the cautionary tale. The cautionary tale is what happens to the founders who don't notice the pattern until it's too late to act on it.

**Where are you building, and has your calculus on location changed in the last two years? I want to hear from the founders who've already made the move — and the ones who are still deciding.**
source_story_title: Larry Page Officially Leaves California Amid Wealth Tax Fears
source_story_summary: Paul Graham reports that Larry Page has genuinely relocated out of California — not to Florida as a tax domicile maneuver, but as a permanent departure. Graham frames this as a direct consequence of California's proposed wealth tax, which hasn't even been enacted yet. The chilling effect alone has already cost the state Page's physical presence and all future tax revenue generated by one of the world's wealthiest individuals.

# The Engineering Team You Have Today Is Already Obsolete

Not because your engineers aren't talented. Because the baseline just moved — and most leadership teams haven't updated their assumptions.

Paul Graham recently flagged a data point circulating among experienced programmers: roughly 1,000 lines of code per hour using AI tooling. What caught my attention wasn't the number. It was his observation that the same stat posted six months ago split audiences between skeptics and believers. The debate has largely ended. The skeptics lost.

That's the actual signal. Not the productivity metric — the velocity of normalization.

---

**The competitive gap is compounding, not static.**

If your team isn't operating at or near this output level, you're not just behind — you're falling further behind every sprint cycle. Competitive disadvantage in software build velocity doesn't plateau. It compounds. Every week your team ships at legacy speed, the teams using AI tooling extend their lead. This isn't a gap you close with a hiring push. You close it by changing how your existing engineers work.

---

**Your headcount model is built on outdated physics.**

If you're in a fundraise right now, or planning one, your engineering headcount projections deserve a hard look. The assumptions baked into most models — how many engineers you need to hit a feature roadmap, how long a build cycle takes — were calibrated in a pre-AI-tooling world. If 1,000 LOC per hour is becoming a realistic floor for experienced AI-assisted developers, the ratio of engineers to output has fundamentally shifted. Investors who understand this will pressure-test you on it. You should pressure-test yourself first.

---

**Adoption isn't happening automatically — it has to be mandated.**

Here's what I see consistently: organizations that "allow" AI tooling adoption get incremental results. Organizations that mandate and structure it — standardized tools, shared prompting practices, integration into the development workflow by default — get transformational results. The difference isn't access. It's operational discipline around adoption. Leaving it to individual engineers to figure out on their own is how you get 20% of the productivity gain while carrying 100% of the coordination overhead.

---

**The hiring implication nobody wants to say out loud.**

If your senior engineers are generating dramatically more output per hour, your staffing ratio assumptions change. That doesn't automatically mean fewer engineers. It means the engineers you hire need to be capable of leveraging these tools at a high level — because the productivity floor for what counts as a "contributing" engineer just rose. Junior hires who can't operate effectively with AI tooling are not the same asset they were two years ago. Your hiring bar and your onboarding model need to reflect that reality.

---

The teams that treat this as a tool upgrade will capture marginal gains. The teams that treat this as a fundamental restructuring of how software gets built will capture the market.

The window where this is a competitive advantage is closing. Once every serious engineering team is operating at this baseline, it becomes table stakes — and the teams that delayed are permanently behind on the features, the product surface, and the institutional knowledge built during the gap.

**Where is your team actually operating right now — and what's your plan to close the distance? Drop it in the comments.**
source_story_title: AI Code Generation Hitting ~1,000 Lines Per Hour for Experienced Programmers
source_story_summary: Paul Graham relays a data point from an experienced programmer now generating roughly 1,000 lines of code per hour using AI tooling. Graham notes that a similar stat posted six months ago split audiences evenly between skeptics and believers, and is now gauging whether that ratio has shifted — implying mainstream adoption may be catching up to early adopters.
